In the global race to deploy autonomy at scale, constraints increasingly sit outside defence budgets – in AI capex, energy and critical minerals. • Drones are entering a hyper-growth phase. That new ecosystem carries macro significance, with three key implications: 1. It spans four budgets – defence, AI capex, energy and minerals – with the latter three emerging as new constraints. This “28th regime” is designed to facilitate innovative firms and startups to scale. While EU Inc. is certainly an improvement on the cost of setting up a business in the EU, the new regime would not address the fragmentation of national legal systems as firms operating in different member states will still need to navigate different tax, commercial and administrative regulations. The 28th regime is set to be finalized by the end of 2026. The Council also agreed to set the Savings and Investment Union (SIU) to complete its first main achievement with the finalisation of “Phase One” by June 2026, focusing on integrated market supervision, securitization, and harmonized insolvency rules. To prevent delays, and in a key change from the past, the Commission agreed with the Council to use “enhanced cooperation” (i.e. allowing a group of at least nine states to move forward) if a full consensus of 27 states cannot be reached on the key initiatives to foster competitiveness. This reform, if delivered as planned, will set a new landscape for the European Competitiveness Fund, a newly proposed central pillar for the 2028–2034 Multiannual Financial Framework (MFF) - the EU budget - currently under negotiation. The proposed fund provides approximately EUR 400bn in support of strategic investments

records.text: From AI Chatbots to AI Agents The current Artificial Intelligence technology (e.g. ChatGPT and Google Gemini) is based on large language models (LLMs), which – via AI chatbots – provide single-step replies to tackle relatively simple problems – even forecasts are addressed in a fairly “linear” way, adopting fairly simple logic. The Agentic AI technology adopts a multi-step approach, which can tackle larger workflows and more complex problems by breaking them down into smaller tasks. AAI tools operate several models simultaneously, and evaluate intermediate results in a constant feedback loop. This is why most experts expect AAI to become the standard in enterprise applications, as more suitable tools to replicate human reasoning. From Traditional AI to Agentic AI Traditional AI, as commonly used today, primarily focuses on specific tasks such as pattern recognition, prediction, classification, and natural language processing. These systems are often reactive, requiring explicit human input for each task, and operate within predefined boundaries. By contrast, Agentic AI is based on several models working in parallel, in a constant feedback loop. Similar to the reasoning of a human brain, AI Agents can interpret an objective, break it down into smaller tasks, set a workflow, draw on external models, and continuously evaluate intermediate results, before producing a final outcome. In that sense, these systems are more proactive and better suited for complex, multi-step problems.

records.text: Japan Economics 23 March 2026 Citi Research 2 First tally of Shunto spring wage negotiations: A strong start The first tally of Shunto spring wage negotiation results shows an average wage hike agreed upon thus far of 5.26%. This is slightly lower than the historic 5.46% increase agreed upon as of the first-round last year but marks a third consecutive year of 5%+ hikes. We think the result is strong and should help the trend for wage hikes to be firmly established (Figure 1). The base pay increase (excluding seniority pay hikes) was 3.85% (+3.84% in the first-round last year). In light of rising inflation and ongoing labor shortages, large companies with strong earnings have been proactively meeting labor unions’ strident demands, which seek to defend daily livelihoods and secure real wage growth. The most-watched SMEs—those with fewer than 300 union members—agreed to increase wages by 5.05% and base-pay by 3.54% (Figure 2). Compared with last year’s final tally (+4.65% and +3.49%, respectively), wage hikes picked up again this year. In our view, SMEs have no choice but increase wages defensively to secure and retain workers as they are faced with even deeper labor shortages than their large counterparts. In fact, workers at large companies moderated their demand this year to +5.88% from +6.04% last year in contrast to a larger pay increase demanded by SME workers (+6.64% this year vs. +6.57% last year). We see 6 Ps driving/constraining AI/datacenter power demand growth: Pervasiveness of AI, Productivity of AI chips/servers/models, Price of power, Policy including permitting/community affairs, Parts availability and People availability. Arguably the most important driver of growth is Pervasiveness — with lack of clarity over the breadth and adoption of AI solutions continuing to drive debates around power demand and equity positioning. Despite upward revisions to hyperscaler Capex + R&D budgets over the last three months, we continue to see tailwinds for the datacenter power supply chain stocks. One of the three key catalysts needed for AI to move from the more thematic Appraisal / Hopes & Dreams Phase to the more stock-specific Execution Phase is when AI demand for tokens/compute becomes defined. We do not believe we are at that point, as large-scale use cases such as Agentics continue to be tested. For more details, please see our February 23, 2026 report, AI/Data Center Power Demand: How rising hyperscaler reinvestment impacts the 6 Ps driving power growth/constraints, led by our GS SUSTAIN team. They have pushed out the peak in Brent prices accordingly and now see a slower subsequent decline, as strategic reserves and other storage will need to be refilled. Moreover, the risks remain heavily skewed toward worse outcomes that feature much higher prices, both for the peak and the longer term. In a severely adverse scenario, damage to energy infrastructure reduces global production capacity for years to come. 2. Higher energy prices will boost global headline inflation sharply in the next 1-2 months. Although the impact should partly reverse once the Strait does reopen, our country-specific rules of thumb imply that the shock will add 0.8pp to global headline inflation over the next year under our baseline and 2pp under our severely adverse scenario. Our estimates are biggest in Europe because of the added shock to home heating costs and power bills from higher natural gas prices, and smallest in China which relies more on coal and electricity than on oil and gas in transportation and home heating. So this time around, we are already seeing policymakers correct for that in a hawkish direction. A key lesson from those past crises is that central banks correct for the perceived errors of the last crisis. So as we face another inflation shock, central banks want to avoid the criticisms of 2022 that they’re too relaxed about inflation, and we can see how that’s informing the response today, with more hawkish rhetoric for a given level of inflation: n First, there’s more reluctance to “look through” the inflation than there was in 2022, despite the fact inflation is actually starting from a lower base today. n Second, there’s already discussion about rate hikes (which markets are pricing), rather than the more reactive approach of 2022, when rates didn’t rise until inflation was already more than triple the Fed and ECB’s targets. records.text: Risks to Our Near-Term Price Forecasts Remain Skewed to the Upside To be sure, a scenario of a quick resolution of the conflict would likely lower our 56 EUR/MWh ($19/mmBtu) Summer (Apr-Oct) 2026 TTF forecast by 16 UR/MWh to near 40 EUR/MWh, consistent with TTF incentivizing maximizing gas-to-coal switching through end-Oct26. However, on net we see risks to our forecast skewed to the upside. Specifically, we estimate that an adverse scenario, where Strait of Hormuz energy flows are at exceptionally low levels for a total of 10 weeks, vs our 6-week base case1, would lift our Summer 2026 TTF forecast by 33 EUR/MWh to 89 EUR/MWh ($30/mmBtu), to further increase demand destruction in and outside of Europe. Lastly, in a severely adverse scenario where, in addition to a longer Hormuz disruption, the ramp up in LNG flows is slower, at eight weeks (vs six), and the long-term damage to Qatari infrastructure is larger, at 20 mtpa (vs 13 mtpa), we think this would require sizable and widespread LNG demand destruction, likely achieved with TTF above 100 EUR ($34/mmBtu) throughout this summer. 1 This would imply LNG flows through Hormuz at zero through early May, followed by a gradual recovery (up to 66 mtpa, given Qatar’s infrastructure damage) through late June. records.text: Executive Summary Agentic AI (AAI) is a much more energy-intensive technology than the current AI chatbots (ChatGPT, Google Gemini); we estimate that each +10pp increase in AAI queries vs baseline expectations (20-30% by 2030-35) could boost datacenter needs by +c.25% vs current projections in the US and Europe. A gradual shift towards Agentic AI would provide a further boost to power consumption, creating tailwinds for Utilities such as stronger organic growth in electricity infrastructure, rising returns in renewables and higher margins in FlexGen. This provides further support to our view that the Utility industry is at the start of an “Earnings Super-Cycle”, which is likely to trigger positive earnings revisions and further multiple expansion. Our favorite European and US plays on this theme include: RWE, Solaria, Enel, PPC, Naturgy, Engie and Siemens Energy in Europe, and NEE, AEP , XEL, and DUK in the US. Agentic AI: what’s coming is far more energy-intensive The current AI tools – chatbots such as ChatGPT or Google Gemini – are based on large language models that provide single-step replies to solve relatively simple problems, while minimizing latency and costs. Agentic AI can tackle complex problems by breaking them down into smaller tasks, while running several models simultaneously in a constant feedback loop. records.text: We Downgrade our European Forecasts Further and Now Expect Two ECB Hikes Given the ongoing conflict in Iran, our commodities team further raised their energy price forecasts. The team now expects shipping through the Strait of Hormuz to remain at only 5% of normal levels for 6 weeks (vs 3 weeks before), followed by a gradual 1-month recovery. They now see a Brent oil price peak of $115 in April and upgrade our 2026Q4 forecast to $80 (vs. $71 before). They likewise lift (see here) their TTF gas price forecast to average 72 EUR/MWh in Q2 (vs. 63 EUR/MWh before) and raise their Q4 forecast to 40 EUR/MWh (vs. 34 EUR/MWh before). Our commodities team sees ongoing upside risks to energy prices and they have laid out two upside price scenarios. In their new adverse scenario, Brent prices average $100 in 2026Q4. In a severely adverse scenario with significant infrastructure damage, Brent remains above $100 through 2027H1. Our commodities team also sees downside risk as the US Administration could end military action at any point, which would likely sharply reduce the risk premium. While not our base case, they don’t rule out US export restrictions, which would widen the Brent-WTI price gap further. Euro area: We Now Expect Two ECB Hikes Using our existing forecast framework, which incorporates both energy price changes and the recent meaningful tightening in European financial conditions, we downgrade Euro area growth by a further 0.3pp this year. This takes the peak level hit to 0.7

We also raise our UK inflation estimates. We now see headline inflation at 3.2% in 2026Q3 in our new baseline (vs 2.7% before), with a larger increase in the Ofgem price cap and more upwards pressure on road fuel prices than in our previous estimates. We have also revised up our 2026H2 core inflation forecast by around 0.15pp, with a peak of 2.6% in 2026Q4. We would expect UK headline inflation to rise to 4% later this year in the adverse scenario, and around 5% in the severe case. Our model implies core inflation would rebound to 2.9% in the adverse scenario and 3.5% in the severely adverse scenario. We then assess how these updated inflation and output gap paths could affect monetary policy. A simple policy rule specified in differences that respond to spot inflation points to policy tightening ahead, with one 25bp increase under our baseline forecasts and more notable tightening in the adverse and severely adverse scenarios. The sharp fall in gold is perhaps the best signal that momentum is moving in favor of the US in this conflict more than the popular view would suggest. Importantly, the S&P 500/gold ratio also bottomed when the conflict started and has made an impulsive 12% move higher that has triggered some buy signals on our technical work. In the US (and globally), the rally in crude oil prices is understating the true increase in costs to consumers. When we look at ‘all-in’ crude oil and product premiums (using consumption weights for the various products), we can see that total prices have increased an extra $20/bbl ytd, over and above the ytd increase in the WTI price of $40/bbl. The US ‘all-in’ price is now >$120/bbl, while the world estimated ‘all-in’ price is almost $140/bbl. Indeed, product premiums in today’s dollars are around their all-time highs of the early 2010s. This is because the ongoing oil shock has impacted both crude and product supplies, driving up both crude and product premiums, in contrast to the 1970s shocks which in general affected crude oil supply more than the refined products markets (in fact we saw negative product premiums in the late 1970s). records.text: 95 Aluminium – Low inventory cover leaves the market exposed to disruptions Source: Citi Research, Wood Mackenzie, SMM, Bloomberg ■ The aluminium market entered the latest Middle East disruption from an already fragile position. Inventory cover has been eroded by years of declining spare capacity outside China, and the recent seasonal build in China only temporarily lifts global weeks of consumption. Under our base case disruption scenario, inventory cover is likely to fall materially through year end-faster than in the moderate scenario, leaving the market increasingly exposed to any further supply shocks. ■ Historically, similar inventory levels have coincided with significantly higher aluminium prices. European all-in prices reached around $4,500/t in real terms during prior tight-market episodes such as 2005–06 and the 2022 energy crisis. This compares with roughly $3,900/t currently (based on LME ~$3,400/t and a ~$490/t European DP premium), implying meaningful upside if inventories tighten further under a prolonged disruption scenario. However, these estimates should be interpreted with caution, as LNG price movements also reflect demand conditions. Such set-ups typically resolve positively for equity investors. De-ratings only get worse in a recession or when the Fed is actually tightening via rates and/or balance sheet, neither of which is likely to occur in our view. The war is still a major topic of concern and uncertainty, but markets have a way of discounting such events very efficiently—as we showed last week, the VIX started rising with crude in January. Historically, stock prices in real (gold) terms tend to bottom just when conflicts seem to be peaking and conditions “feel” the worst and/or hopeless. While we're not old enough to recall what it felt like when the US actively engaged in WWII in the spring of 1942, we're pretty sure it didn't make people feel "bullish." We do remember when the US invaded Iraq in the spring of 2003 and the extreme contention there was around that decision, especially given the unfavorable results in our last ground war in Vietnam. The "shock and awe" of that first day indeed marked the end of a very long bear market that had begun almost 3 years prior. In short, markets have a way of processing events long before it's a headline. records.text: Putting Private Credit Risks in Macroeconomic Context Concerns about the outlook for private credit have increased recently and driven a pickup in retail investor redemptions from several funds. In today’s Daily, we frame the potential macroeconomic impact of private credit losses on economywide lending and GDP growth. The private credit industry has grown quickly in recent years, and it currently holds about $1.7tn in levered loans to the corporate sector, or 4% of all credit to the private non-financial sector (Exhibit 1).1 While the sector has grown, it is still small relative to the rest of the financial system—for context, residential mortgages amounted to about 45% of credit to the private non-financial sector in the runup to the 2008 financial crisis. There is limited visibility into these loans, but available indicators suggest that loan performance as of 2025Q4 has remained broadly in line with its average since 2023. The share of underperforming loans in private credit companies’ investment portfolios has increased slightly in 2025H2 but remained below 2023 levels (left side of Exhibit 2). And while the share of loans with payment-in-kind (PIK) options—the ability to issue additional securities to pay interest and a potential indicator of borrower stress short of outright default—is higher now than it was before 2023, this mostly reflects the fact that more recent loans have been originated with a PIK option, rather than migrating into PIK because of borrower stress

We continue to expect Norges Bank to stay on hold at 4% this year, with semi-annual cuts over next years to an unchanged terminal rate of 3.25%. Although the shock is both growth- and inflation-promoting for Norway, we see a higher hurdle for Norges Bank to restart the hiking cycle from an already restrictive 4% policy rate. records.text: What’s coming in AI is far more energy-intensive The multi-model, constant feedback looping approach of Agentic AI models requires much more computational power and therefore has much larger energy needs. Over the past three years, AI queries have gained strong efficiencies. When compared to a consumption of 2.7 Wh/query at inception, current ChatGPT and Google Gemini models consume c.0.30 Wh; although this is a c.90% reduction in energy intensity in less than five years, it is still c.10% higher than a non-AI Google search. A paper by Microsoft and other articles suggest that Agentic AI could be c.15-50x more energy-intensive than AI Chatbots. We take a more conservative stance in our analysis, and assume >50% efficiency gains at the low end of this range, which still implies 6x higher energy intensity. This could imply – depending on the rate of adoption – much greater than anticipated energy needs. This is also consistent with interviews by the main Tech founders at companies including OpenAI and Google Deepmind. AI chatbots’ energy efficiency has positively surprised Early versions of AI chatbots, such as ChatGPT at its 2022 launch, were substantially more energy-intensive than “traditional” search engines, consuming around 10x more power per query. records.text: Historically, equity downturns since 2000 have been driven primarily by increasing equity risk premia (see page 9 for methodology), rather than fundamentals, at least in the initial phase. Typically, fundamental estimates are revised downward after markets have already declined by at least 20% from peak levels. While interest rates tend to be more reactive in the short term, their contribution to equity returns during these downturns varies depending on the circumstances. For example, the 2022 rates had a significant impact on equity performance, unlike 2007 and 2011, where revenue and earnings per share were more influential. Upon examining the end of these downturns, a similar pattern emerges, where equity risk premium (ERP) leads the recovery rather than fundamental revisions. Investors tend to be quicker to discount a potential recovery, and analysts are faster to revise numbers upward during the recovery phase than downward during the downturn. Notably, rate moves often have a positive return attribution to equity returns prior to the start of the recovery, suggesting that monetary policy plays a crucial role in facilitating the exit from these periods of decline. The divergence between the US and EU markets’ return attribution over the past two years is also noteworthy. European equities have been largely driven by ERP, with fundamentals still awaiting an inflection point. In contrast, the US market has been primarily driven by earnings upgrades. While the uncertainty about the duration of disruptions remains high, the 6-weeks assumption for peak Hormuz disruptions sits between a) the 4 to 6 weeks range for the military operation cited by US policymakers and b) the median length of the conflict currently reflected in prediction markets.1 Because our 6-weeks (i.e. 5% of normal flows till April 11) assumption corresponds to SoH flows edging up above 5% and because Iran already allows some selective passage, SoH flows are likely to exceed 5% before the conflict ends. records.text: Gauging China’s exposure to Hormuz disruptions We first assess China’s exposure to Hormuz disruptions through import dependence, energy consumption by source, price transmission mechanisms, and the direct weight of energy in CPI and PPI baskets. While China is a large net importer of energy, its vulnerability to supply disruptions is more nuanced than headline import dependence suggests. China’s crude oil import dependence is around 70%, with roughly 45% of imports linked to flows through the Strait of Hormuz, implying about 30% of total oil supply in China is exposed to Hormuz disruptions. By contrast, natural gas exposure is more limited. Although China’s natural gas import dependence is about 40%, pipeline gas accounts for a rising share of imports, while liquefied natural gas (LNG) represents only about half of total gas imports. Among LNG imports, around 30% originated from Qatar, implying that only around 6% of total gas supply in China is exposed to Hormuz disruptions. Overall, this suggests that China’s direct exposure to oil supply disruptions is much higher than for natural gas. In addition, China’s energy consumption and power generation mix suggest that it is less exposed to energy supply shortage from Hormuz disruptions than most major economies and Asian peers. As shown in Exhibit 2, oil and gas account for around 20% and 10% of China’s primary energy consumption as of 2024, respectively, much lower than the global averages of 33% and 26%. The demographic profile of the sample is especially important considering that surveys suggest that younger people disapprove of the current government more than older voters (see Figure 15). If a poll overrepresents younger respondents (as is the case with the Datafolha and Quaest surveys in Figure 14), we can assume that the poll will tend to give lower performance for the incumbent, and vice versa if a poll overrepresents older voters. Methodology can also introduce a bias. Telephone or online surveys rely on respondents who are willing to answer the questionnaire and are therefore likely to be more politically engaged. In-person face-to-face street interviews approach people randomly and are thus more likely to reflect the views of the average voter — many of whom, research suggests, become attentive only close to election day. The three best-performing pollsters from the second round in 2022 all deploy in-person interviews (see Figure 16). From the 2010 elections, Vox Populi and CNI had joined this group. In 2022, the field became more crowded, with 14 pollsters gauging how Brazilians would vote for president. With that context, we examine 12 polls that consistently released data throughout the 2022 election, aiming to assess their accuracy against the final results. In the first round, the two front-runners were generally mis-estimated, especially Jair Bolsonaro, whose support was repeatedly underestimated: his vote share in opinion polls was, on average, 3.6pp lower than the actual result. The largest discrepancies came from Ipes​p, Quaest, and Datafolha, each undershooting Bolsonaro by about 7–8 pp. CNT and PoderData were the most accurate overall. In the second round, CNT again proved the most reliable, only 0.2pp off Lula’s winning vote share, followed closely by Paraná and Quaest (0.5pp and 0.8pp, respectively; see Figure 10). Samples can make the difference: We observe variations in virtually every characteristic of the samples — gender, age, region and education (see Figures 11– 14 overleaf) – which is likely to bias a particular pollster’s results depending on the dominant traits of the surveyed population. records.text: 7T2se3r0Ot6kwoPa 7T2se3r0Ot6kwoPa Distributed on: 23/03/2026 09:23:23 GMT Distributed on: 23/03/2026 09:23:23 GMT 23 March 2026 Deutsche Bank Research Global Cross-Discipline Thematic Research Date Why history points towards a hawkish central bank reaction A consistent theme of economic cycles is that policymakers tend to correct (and often overcorrect) for past mistakes. The lessons of the last crisis are always top of mind. This pattern has repeatedly happened with central banks, including with oil shocks. After all, human nature generally tries to avoid making the same mistake twice. Just to take some recent examples: n In the 1970s oil shocks, the general view was that central banks weren’t hawkish enough against the first oil shock of 1973, meaning inflation expectations became unanchored. So when the second oil shock hit in 1979, policymakers like Paul Volcker were much tougher, delivering a strongly hawkish response to deal with inflation. n After the sluggish GFC recovery from 2008, many felt a more dovish response could have sped that up. So when the next major recession hit with Covid in 2020, central banks pivoted much faster towards rate cuts and QE, and their forward guidance signalled ultra-accommodative policy for years to come. n Today we are presented with another oil shock, similar to 2022 in many respects. records.text: 23 March 2026 Thematic Research Page 6 Deutsche Bank AG In both the US and the Euro Area, inflation was more than double the central banks’ target for two full years. And even though inflation fell back from its peak levels in 2022, it’s still lingered above target in many countries. For example, US inflation has been above target for five years now, and in the Euro Area, core CPI has been above 2% since late-2021. So this context has led to extensive discussions about whether high inflation could have been prevented, for instance by having done less stimulus in the pandemic, or tightening policy earlier than they did. For today, we can already see how that experience is informing the response to the current energy crisis. n First, unlike in 2022, there’s now an explicit acknowledgement that inflation has been above target for an extensive period. Indeed, Fed Chair Powell said in his March press conference that looking through energy shocks has “always been dependent on inflation expectations remaining well anchored”, and he also mentioned the “broader context of five years now of inflation above target.” n Second, we can see how there is more reluctance to “look through” the inflation than there was in 2021-22. 44 Nuclear fuel prices (SWU) are still rising, pointing to higher U3O8 prices Source : UxC, Citi Research Exactly two years ago, uranium prices traded above $100/lb after which prices traded down to $60/lb for the following year, which we have been suggesting as a great opportunity to get long. Since summer 2025, spot prices have been rising and now prices are settled in mid-90’s, and at a slight discount to the term price of $90/lb. We expect term prices continue to increase, while spot would obviously be more volatile and trading above $100 for the next 2 years. As a base case, we also don’t expect waivers on Russia’s LEU to be extended beyond 2027, which will tighten the SWU prices even further. Overall, we expect uranium supply to increase by 11.6 million lbs (from prev 17 million lbs increase projected) in 2026 y/y. The total mine supply is projected to hit 175 million lbs this year. However, this is subject to revision depending on how long SoH will stay closed, and sulfuric acid availability. We estimate that total utility demand for 2026 will be close to 194 million lbs, with a significant gap being filled in by secondary supplies as it was done in the past. records.text: 2 Japan Watch | 23 March 2026 Supports BoJ’s April hike, but with few new implications The strong FY26 Shunto wage outcomes shown in today’s first-round response suggest that the mechanism the BoJ emphasizes, in which wages and prices rise moderately in interaction with each other, is likely to remain intact going forward. In particular, the solid wage increases among SMEs, which Governor Ueda highlighted as a key focal point of this year’s Shunto at the press conference following last week’s Monetary Policy Meeting, provide support for the BoJ’s rate hike decision at the upcoming April meeting (see BoJ review: Moving toward the next hike despite a clouded outlook 19 March). That said, the BoJ had already anticipated firm Shunto wage outcomes as of last December, based on what it described as the “initial momentum.” As such, today’s results do not constitute new information, and are unlikely to materially alter the BoJ’s expected path of policy rate hikes. What’s next Today’s first-round tabulation covers 19.6% of unions and approximately 48.2% of union members in terms of wage outcomes. The next step will be to assess wage hikes across a broader range of firms in the second round of responses on 27 March and the third round on 3 April. In particular, the 3 April release will include detailed breakout tables, shedding light on wage developments by sector. , logistics and resupply. In general, these roles are supported by mission-specific platforms, with designs varying by mission. Systems span fuel- powered and electric propulsion, single-use and reusable platforms, and vary widely in speed, range, size, and endurance. Against this backdrop, we find it useful to group defence drones into two broad categories that differ in role and scale: high-value specialised drones and low-cost highly scalable drones (Figure 4). This distinction is important, as it captures the trade-off between performance and scale shaping modern battlefield use. High-value specialised drones offer advanced systems but are expensive, often costing millions per unit. At the other end of the spectrum, low-cost scalable drones trade performance for affordability and mass deployment, supporting short- range and often one-way missions, with prices typically in the $20k-$50K range per unit. Drones range from fully operator-controlled to highly autonomous systems – though most still rely on human piloting and are not fully autonomous. Even so, AI already sits at the core of drone functionality. In higher-value platforms, it supports flight assistance, communications, and system coordination, while in lower-cost drones it enables collision guidance, navigation, and multi-drone coordination – allowing simpler hardware to operate effectively at scale. Price/earnings multiples peaked on October 29th of last year, making this correction almost 5 months in duration. More impressively, the forward P/E for the S&P 500 is down approximately 15%, which is a significant outcome historically (Exhibit 1 ). records.text: 21 Strait of Hormuz flows Q&A • Q: How much oil and products usually flow through the Strait of Hormuz? • A: Recent normal flows (2025) were ~15-m b/d of crude oil and 5.5-m b/d of products, of which 1.6-m b/d was LPG, 1.2-m b/d naphtha, 1-m b/d diesel, and 0.3-m b/d gasoline, 20% of global seaborne oil trade flows. • Q: Given current disruptions, how much is flowing through the Strait currently, as of early Mar’26? • A: Recent reported oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz are reported to be around 1-m b/d of crude oil (though they may have picked up to 2mb/d from Iran), and 0.5-m b/d of products, or ~90% below recent norms, per ship tracking, though this is very likely to be undercounted given vessels may have turned off transponders to avoid detection, and we ballpark a 70-90% reduction in flows. This drop has come as physical risks and freight/insurance costs spiked. • Q: How much effective alternative capacity is there for Gulf oil producers to bypass the Strait? • A: Perhaps only ~3-5-m b/d incrementally, mainly on the Saudi East-West pipeline, which may have an estimated 5-7-m b/d of capacity, with pre-existing flows of 2-m b/d. The UAE has the ADCOP pipeline to Fujairah with ~2-m b/d capacity, but may already be fully utilized. Iraq might have 0.4-m b/d of additional flows northwards, but faces domestic political constraints. records.text: Prices Drift Higher During Disruption with Risk Premium Due to uncertainty around the duration of the shock and assuming Hormuz flows remain at 5% through April 10, prices are likely to trend higher over that period until the market gains confidence that a lengthy disruption is unlikely and converges to our “after the shock” fair-value based model. We now expect Brent to average $110 in March-April (vs. $98 prior)—-up 62% from the 2025 annual average. We have nudged down our March Brent forecast to $105 (vs. $110 prior), which implies an average Brent price for the rest of the month of just over $120. We have upgraded our Brent April forecast to $115 (vs. $85 prior) as a longer disruption supports the risk premium for longer. We forecast WTI to average $98 in March and $105 in April, with the market putting some probability on US exports keeping the Brent-WTI price gap wide. From a Local to a Global Shock The price of Brent nearby futures in March has risen less than we had expected despite still very low Hormuz flows, reflecting physical and financial factors. On the physical side, the largest oil supply shock ever is still mostly a local shock leading to extreme declines in oil in transit and tightness in Asia (which typically accounts for 95% Hormuz imports), especially for heavier refined products such as jet fuel. records.text: 23 March 2026 Thematic Research Page 2 Deutsche Bank AG n In the 1970s, central banks were widely judged to have been too slow after the first oil shock in 1973, allowing inflation expectations to drift higher. When the second oil shock hit in 1979, policymakers—most notably Paul Volcker—responded far more forcefully. n After the post-2008 recovery proved sluggish, many concluded policy should have been more aggressive. So when Covid hit in 2020, central banks moved quickly with cuts, QE and strong guidance signalling prolonged accommodation. n Today, we face another energy-driven inflation shock, reminiscent in some respects of 2022. But in 2022, central banks were criticised for initially underestimating inflation and moving too late. This time, they appear determined not to repeat that mistake—and the bias is already more hawkish. That shows up in three ways. First, there is less willingness to “look through” the inflation impulse than in 2022, even though inflation is starting from a lower base. Second, rate hikes are already being discussed and priced, rather than delayed until inflation is far above target. Third, the broader context matters: inflation has been above target for several years, with Chair Powell acknowledging “five years now of inflation above target,” at his recent press conference. Running our proxy for the March 20 staff baseline through our policy rules using a simplified version of the ECB’s macro model points to about two rate hikes. Consistent with this, the post-meeting communication has been hawkish with Bundesbank President Nagel calling for an April hike if energy price pressures do not abate and Irish Governor Makhlouf arguing that the staff’s baseline already assumes two rate hikes. A shift towards Agentic AI would incrementally boost power consumption, creating tailwinds for Utilities such as stronger organic growth in electricity infrastructure, rising returns in renewables and higher margins in FlexGen. This further supports our view that the Utility industry is at the start of an “Earnings Super-Cycle”, which is likely to trigger positive earnings revisions and multiple expansion. Agentic AI: what’s coming is far more energy-intensive. The current AI tools – chatbots such as ChatGPT or Google Gemini – are based on large language models that are optimized to solve relatively simple problems at the minimum cost. According to tech literature, Agentic AI could be c.15-50x more energy-intensive than AI chatbots. Each +10pp in Agentic AI queries could boost datacenter needs by +c.25% vs expectations. records.text: 57 The physical gold market cannot handle wealth shifts into gold Source: Citi Research Estimates, Credit Suisse, Bloomberg The table below illustrates that the physical gold market is too small to handle wealth shifts into gold which has been true for decades. At present, the value of gold supply is around 0.1% of total household wealth (property, equities, bonds, cash, including that managed on their behalf by institutions etc). This means that a 0.1% increase, or 1/1000th shift of household wealth into gold would require a doubling in gold mine supply. An increase from global average levels of 3.7% to 5% would require ~15.5 years of mine supply equivalent to half of all jewellery and bar and coin stocks built over millennia. Clearly, wealth shifts cannot be accommodated, and prices need to do the work to increase the allocation to gold, by encouraging old stockholders to rebalance their portfolio to new holders. Fig. 1: MoF plans to cut long-end issuance as well as T-bill sales Scheduled reductions in super-long JGB issuance: Japan’s Ministry of Finance plans to cut the new 20-, 30- and 40-year JGBs issuance from April. After the 2025 amendment, the amount of discount short-term bonds was increased from JPY40.8trn to JPY49.2trn. In the initial budget for FY2026, however, the amount is slated to fall back to JPY40.8trn – a reduction of JPY8.4trn compared with the FY2025 supplementary budget. The MoF will conduct a mid-year assessment of the issuance plan for FY2026 and onward, and, if necessary, revise the plan within the fiscal year. Should market conditions move sharply before the mid-year assessment and an additional cut in super-long JGB issuance become necessary, there is room to offset the reduction by issuing more Treasury bills, in our view. The fact that the super-long sector can always be trimmed gives market participants a sense of security, which has helped the flattening of the curve from December to February. Overall, the planned supply cut provides a source of support for super-long JGBs. The escalation in the Middle East conflict has also added steepening pressure on the yield curve. records.text: 136 Manganese Ore – Freight rates and restocking to push prices higher Source: Citi Research, Bloomberg, IMnI ■ Base Case (60% probability) – We increase our 0-3mth point price to $5.50/dmtu (previously $4.75/dmtu). We see restocking by end-users and increased freight rates likely to drive ore prices higher. Increased alloy prices are supportive of further price increases. The Middle East conflict has pushed up shipping freight rates higher. Apart from freight rates, higher energy prices are likely to increase trucking costs in South Africa pushing the cost curve for producers. Despite a subdued steel outlook in China, port inventories are at ~40 - 45days of consumption, lower than historical levels limiting price downside. ■ Bull case (20% probability) - We see manganese ore averaging $6/dmtu by 2Q’26, supported by strong China steel demand (especially from long steel products), stronger alloy output, restocking by mills and smelters, steel intensive policy easing measures by China, no resolution to the conflict in Middle East and/or supply disruptions. ■ Bear case (20% probability) - We see manganese ore averaging $5/dmtu by 2Q’26, driven by weaker steel demand in both China and the rest of the world, China alloy smelter cuts, de-escalation in the Middle East, and/or improved supply from major producers. This boosts safety and saves labor – tasks that once required lifting staff with forklifts can be done autonomously by drone. • In the delivery sector, drones offer a potential solution to the long-standing “last-mile” challenge, often the slowest and most expensive part of logistics. The technology is now moving from pilot projects to real operations. Since partnering with Walmart in Dallas–Fort Worth in 2023, Alphabet’s Wing has scaled its Texas operations to thousands of orders per week, with average delivery times of under 19 minutes. Customers can receive everyday items in under 30 minutes through a hub-and-spoke model linking 18 Walmart Supercenters. Operating autonomously beyond visual line of sight, drones could outperform ground delivery on short routes and point to meaningful labour savings at scale. Without AI, low-cost drones would still function, but would be harder to scale, less effective and far more dependent on human operators. With AI, capability shifts more from hardware to software – enabling navigation and paving the way for swarm-based operations, where coordinated groups of drones are deployed together to achieve a shared mission. 5 Setting the stage for AI integration in defence Our analysis indicates a gradual shift toward greater AI incorporation in drones, which is set to become a key application of AI in defence. We observe three trends as AI-enabled drones enter defence systems. First, AI reduces reliance on human pilots, easing constraints on large-scale aerial operations. Second, AI-enabled drone autonomy can improve resilience in environments affected by jamming or signal disruption by supporting on-device navigation and decision- making without continuous human control. Third, drone swarm-based operations are more effective when guided by AI models, allowing groups of drones to coordinate, adapt, and reorganise as missions evolve. A new investment cycle that cuts across defence, AI, energy and minerals Physical AI defence systems, like drones, now sit at the intersection of four budgets: defence, AI capex, energy and minerals. records.text: 23 March 2026 Thematic Research Page 2 Deutsche Bank AG n Third, as in the 1970s context, we know that inflation has generally been above target for several years. Fed Chair Powell himself acknowledged the “broader context of five years now of inflation above target.” So that adds to the risk of another shock un-anchoring expectations, requiring a more hawkish response. Correcting and overcorrecting from history: A few examples The 1970s oil shocks The second oil shock saw a far more forceful monetary policy response given how persistent inflation became after the first shock. Back in 1973, an oil embargo on many Western countries saw oil prices nearly quadruple. Many were pushed into a deep recession, and US CPI inflation peaked at 12.2% afterwards. This was the highest it had been since the immediate aftermath of WWII. Central banks have turned markedly less dovish—and in some cases outright hawkish—in response to rising inflation fears, as media coverage of inflation and the Iranian conflict has intensified (Figure 3). This shift was evident at last week’s central bank meetings, where multiple G10 central banks revised their inflation outlooks higher. Market pricing has responded forcefully, extending the hawkish repricing that began at the onset of the conflict. That said, expectations have not shifted uniformly. For some economies, the conflict has catalysed an entirely new hiking cycle, while in others the outlook has flipped 180 degrees— from anticipated cuts to hikes. While we do not dispute the inflation risks—PriceStats, our daily online measure of inflation, is already showing a sharp uptick in prices reminiscent of 2022—we see asymmetric risks across central banks, and by extension currencies, where inflation is being over‑prioritized relative to growth. records.text: However, these estimates can be misleading, as oil price movements reflect a combination of demand- and supply-driven forces (see detailed discussions in “Assessing the potential impact of higher oil prices on EM Asia”). Stronger global demand tends to generate larger and more persistent inflationary pressures, while supply-driven shocks are more likely to produce front-loaded and shorter-lived effects. To address this issue, we isolate oil supply shocks using the proxy variable constructed by Känzig (2021), which identifies exogenous supply-driven oil price movements based on high-frequency future price changes around OPEC announcements. Re-estimating the inflation responses using supply-driven oil price changes, we find the magnitude of the inflation impact is smaller than suggested by the VAR approach shown in Exhibit 4, with PPI rising by around 60bp on average over the first 12 months, and headline CPI by around 10bp, following a 10% oil price increase (Exhibit 5). The response is also more front-loaded: PPI inflation rises modestly initially (25bp), overshoots after two months to around 90bp, then gradually moderates to 30bp by the 12-month horizon. Headline CPI response remains significantly smaller but follows a similar dynamic pattern, rising modestly on impact (around 6bp), peaking at around 18bp after 2 months, and then gradually fading. Upside Risks From Longer Disruption and Persistent Supply Losses Under two risk scenarios where Hormuz flows remain at only 5% for a total of 10 weeks, daily Brent prices exceed their 2008 $147 peak. In the adverse scenario, Mideast supply recovers on reopening without persistent production losses. In the adverse scenario, Brent rises to a monthly average of $140 in April (a monthly record), and then converges to $100 in 2026Q4 and to $90 in 2027Q4 (Exhibit 2) as demand and supply respond to high prices. The severely adverse scenario considers a persistent 2mb/d loss in Mideast production. Looking at the 5 prior largest supply shocks of the past 50 years, we estimate an average hit to production in the affected country of 42% after 4 years, often due to infrastructure damage and low investment. For context, Iran and the 7 other Persian Gulf countries together produced 30% of global crude in 2025. In the severely adverse scenario, Brent spikes and then converges to $115 in 2026Q4 and to $100 in 2027Q4 given a strong price response of demand and supply. records.text: blue line in Exhibit 7).5 Exhibit 8 compares our latest PPI inflation forecast with the pre-Iran conflict baseline, which shows higher oil prices mainly lift PPI inflation in 2026. Oil-led PPI reflation likely to stay in upstream sectors The current inflation upturn is largely driven by higher raw material prices and is therefore concentrated in upstream sectors, rather than reflecting a broad-based improvement in demand. We regress headline PPI inflation and the contributions from upstream and downstream sectors on oil price changes. The relative magnitudes of the estimated slopes provide an indicative decomposition of how oil-driven reflation is distributed across sectors. Exhibit 9 shows that around 80% of PPI reflation is from upstream industrial sectors, including energy, metals, chemicals and construction materials, despite their relatively small share in the PPI basket (around 30%).6 Meanwhile, the transmission from PPI inflation to core CPI remains muted, with a 1% increase in PPI inflation translating into only around 5bp of core CPI inflation, implying limited spillovers into the services sector. We further examine the pass-through from higher oil prices to core CPI and short-term inflation expectations (proxied by 1-year ahead consensus headline CPI forecasts), and find limited spillovers: a 10% supply-driven increase in oil prices raises core CPI by around 5bp, with effects remaining modest for several months before fading. records.text: Alex Swade Michael Metcalfe 23 March 2026 Classification: Premium Material 1 Insights Information Classification: General FX Execution Insights – Stagflation, liquidity and intervention Figure 1: FX turbulence continues Figure 2: Volume (5-day, percentiles) Weekly Insights: With hopes of a quick end to the conflcit in the Middle East fading, the market narrative is shifting to the potential economic consequences and stagflation in particular. The knee jerk reaction from interest rate markets has been that central banks will b e hawkish in their response and their commentary in the past week has reinforced rather than calmed this. This has potentially important knock on effects for global liquidity, FX markets but also intervention risks. Volume: Both G10 and EM FX volumes remain elevated, which is to be expected given higher turbulence. The one exception is USDJPY, where volumes were close to the bottom decile. This could reflect concerns about intervention to prevent further (inflationary) JPY we akness in this new stagflationary environment. records.text: cial conditions. So when the next major recession hit with the Covid-19 pandemic in 2020, there was no such hesitation. For instance, the Fed delivered an unscheduled 50bp rate cut in early March, and less than two weeks’ later they announced another unscheduled 100bp rate and a fresh round of QE. Unlike 2008, there was no discussion of normalizing policy anytime soon either. Indeed, the December 2020 dot plot still had the median dot unchanged at end-2023, suggesting most FOMC members didn’t want to hike rates until at least 2024. Meanwhile at the ECB, there was a much more forceful response too, announcing the Pandemic Emergency Purchase Programme (PEPP) in March 2020, which ultimately had a total envelope of €1.85tn by December 2020. Central banks even made their frameworks more dovish in the pandemic period, explicitly tolerating higher inflation than before. At the Fed, they moved towards average inflation targeting, which permitted inflation to remain above target after a period of below-target inflation. Meanwhile at the ECB, they raised their inflation target to a symmetric 2% in 2021, having previously been “below, but close to, 2%”. This dovish reaction continued into 2021 and early 2022, informed by the post-GFC experience of very low inflation. So as inflation began to rise in 2021, arguments were put forward as to why this was transitory, driven by factors like supply-chain kinks that would soon normalize. records.text: 89 Aluminium – Structural tightness reinforced by disruption risks Source: Citi Research, Bloomberg, LME We now expect a wider aluminium deficit in 2026, with Middle East disruption deepening what had previously been a modest shortfall. Our base case assumes a ~1.3Mt deficit, driven by logistics-related raw material constraints and broader regional curtailments. Macro conditions remain steady but soft, with demand stabilising across key downstream sectors and a modest improvement in financial conditions. As a result, near-term pricing is increasingly driven by supply-side risks rather than macro momentum. ■ Our base case (50% probability) continues to reflect an emerging structural deficit, with aluminium prices averaging around $3,400/t in 2026 (around $3,450/t in 2Q26). Constrained supply growth and limited ex-China capacity expansion remain the dominant drivers. On top of this, we embed a ~2mth Middle East disruption assumption, affecting roughly 4Mt of smelting capacity via logistics related raw material constraints, triggering broader curtailments and reinforcing the deficit already visible in the market. On the macro side, global growth is steady but unspectacular: monetary policy remains on a gradual easing path, financing conditions improve modestly, and demand from key downstream sectors stabilises. Overall, we see this year’s wage hike result as positive to the extent that it confirms a virtuous circle of wages and prices, which is a necessary precondition for the BoJ to achieve its price stability goal. In our view, the outcome by itself was in line with policymakers’ assumptions and thus will not affect the pace of policy normalization. Moreover, this year’s spring wage negotiations have already reached a final phase, with the escalating Middle East situation hardly factored in. The impact, if any, will probably be reflected in negotiations next spring. If the conflict persists and keeps oil prices elevated, corporate profits will likely be squeezed, making wage hikes more difficult. In this regard, we do not see this year’s wage hike result by itself as convincing grounds to expect an early hike by the BoJ. As we discussed in our BoJ review last week, we think the key to future rate hike decisions will be 1) the situation in the Middle East and 2) the FX market. As long as the Middle East situation remains tense, we think the BoJ is likely to remain on the sidelines. records.text: 108 The global AI/datacentre boom is set to contribute ~200ktpa to copper demand in both 2026 and 2027, before levelling out towards 2030 at ~800ktpa We estimate indirect demand for copper in supporting power infrastructure (grid and generation) beyond the local datacentre site represents ~15% of total datacentre-related demand Copper – Datacentres can add ~200ktpa to Cu demand growth in 2026/27 Source: Citi Research, IEA We believe a continued acceleration in datacentre build-outs over the next two years can drive 200ktpa of copper demand growth through 2026 and 2027. We see this growth tapering out in the late 2020s, at ~800ktpa. The boost to copper consumption from the AI- datacentre thematic over the next couple of years is primarily because of the significant near-to-medium-term growth rates (~45% 2026, ~20% 2027) as datacentres are only a small share of global Cu consumption (1.2% today versus 2.3% projected by 2027); We expect the sector’s contribution to global copper demand growth to fade beyond 2027. It is worth adding that datacentres also have potential to drive global copper demand through the resultant boost to global productivity and growth, although this is difficult to model and longer-term. *Power gen assumes 50% renewable/non-renewable demand split. Residual tariff risk (a potential 15% by 2027 and 30% by 2028) appears to be supporting a continued COMEX-LME premium on forward months, but nearby months are at or below parity which has driven deliveries into US-based LME warehouses. Our base case remains either no US import tariff on refined copper, or an introduction of a phased S232 tariff in June with zero-tariff exemptions granted to key partners (e.g. Chile, Mexico, Canada etc.); A fresh and sustainable reacceleration of copper imports into the US would likely require policy announcements to increase the perceived likelihood and magnitude of possible copper import tariffs, which remains plausible, but not our base case. However, 2s5s has not yet demonstrated an extended bear flattening since the lifting negative rate policy. Therefore, 2s5s10s tended to cheapen up until the actual rate hike and richens back modestly after the hike, such as in December 2025 (Figure 5) and January 2025 (Figure 6). records.text: nd 1.2 1.0 1y, 6m T-bill 49.2 40.8 Gross market supply 178.7 168.5 Japan: JGB supply demand analysis ahead of FY2026 KEY MESSAGES We think the planed supply cut for super-long JGBs by MoF is likely to support long end of JGB curve. While BoJ is expected to cut its JGB purchase up to 25-years sector and domestic demand is likely to concentrate on front end, foreign investors may support this sector. Trade idea: Buy 30y ASW at OIS+58bp, targeting OIS+50bp. Stop-out at OIS+65bp. DV01= 50k/bp. Scheduled reductions in super-long JGB issuance: From April, the Ministry of Finance plans to cut the amount of new 20-, 30- and 40-year JGBs to be issued. The deterioration of the Middle-East situation has put steepening pressure on the yield curve, but the reduction in issuance also provides a source of support for super-long JGBs. The MoF will conduct a mid-year assessment of the issuance plan for FY2026 and onward, and, if necessary, MoF will revise the plan within the fiscal year. So in October 1979, Volcker held an unscheduled Saturday press conference, announcing a shift towards managing the volumes of bank reserves, constraining the growth of the money supply that way. Along with the oil shock, this was enough to push the US economy into a recession starting in early 1980, with the fed funds rate rising to 20% at its peak. This time round, inflation did fall on a durable basis – a key difference with the first oil shock of 1973. But it was precisely because the first oil shock happened, with persistent inflation afterwards, that policymakers had the space for a more forceful response. That context and the perceived mistakes from the first oil shock proved crucial in determining how the second oil shock was dealt with. The GFC (2008) and the Covid-19 pandemic (2020) A sluggish post-GFC recovery meant that when the next big recession hit with Covid-19, policymakers unveiled much quicker and larger stimulus packages, and after years of below-target inflation, they were more cautious about reacting when inflation did re-emerge in 2021-22. 1 A. Our commodity research team highlights upside risks to crude oil prices given the potential for prolonged Hormuz disruptions and damage to energy infrastructure, and they have further raised their crude oil price forecast to $85/bbl from $77/bbl for 2026 full-year average. records.text: 23 March 2026 Thematic Research Page 4 Deutsche Bank AG During the 2008 crisis, fears of another Great Depression led to huge quantities of stimulus, that were unprecedented in a peacetime context. Central banks slashed rates aggressively, with the Fed going to the zero lower bound in late-2008. And with nowhere left to cut rates to, many also launched quantitative easing packages. Similarly on the fiscal side, deficits reached levels unseen since WWII. Yet despite all that, the recovery out of the financial crisis was still very sluggish. In the US, the Fed didn’t hike rates again off the lower bound until 2015, and unemployment didn’t get back to its pre-GFC levels until 2017, almost a decade later. Meanwhile in the Euro Area, the economy deteriorated further after the GFC, as the sovereign crisis then caused another recession. Both inflation and interest rates remained low throughout the 2010s. As the years went on, the perception grew that the recovery had been too sluggish after 2008, and policymakers should have responded more forcefully, particularly given inflation and interest rates were at historically low levels. For instance, arguments grew that interest rates should have been cut more rapidly, with alternative measures like forward guidance used earlier to ease financial conditions. Th e percentiles have the advantage of making no assumptions about the shape of the distribution of the indicators, such as normality. Our use is aimed at being a simple way of ranking flow and positioning indicators relative to their own history. For all of the flow indicators within the Investment Climate, we calculate the percentiles based on the distribution of flows over the last five years using the daily aggregate time periods shown in the tables. Before calculating the percentiles, we constrain the 50 th percentile as equivalent to neutral. Flows above the 50 th percentile, therefore, are all positive and those below the 50th all represent selling of the market in question. A 100th percentile reading represents the strongest buying in five years; and a zero percentile equals the strongest selling. Against this backdrop, near term pricing is increasingly anchored by supply side risks. ■ In our bull scenario (30% probability), prices rise towards $4,000/t as disruption persists or escalates, amplifying an already tight structural backdrop. A prolonged Strait of Hormuz blockage would restrict raw material flows, forcing full shutdowns and extending restart timelines, accelerating inventory drawdowns and widening the deficit into 2027. This is further supported by a broadly benign macro backdrop, where resilient global growth and the market’s ability to absorb higher energy prices sustain demand, allowing supply- side constraints to translate more fully into price upside. ■ In our bear scenario (20% probability), aluminium prices ease towards $2,900/t despite recent disruption. A short-lived disruption allows curtailed capacity to restart more quickly, while the macro backdrop deteriorates; tighter financial conditions, weaker industrial activity, and persistently elevated energy prices feed into a softer economic outlook. Demand growth slows materially, delaying normalisation in consumption. As a result, the supply demand balance loosens relative to expectations, inventory drawdowns stall, and price upside becomes capped. Prepared for Cayla Buettner

Motor fuel accounts for 2.5% of the CPI basket. Combined with the estimated pass-through from global oil prices to domestic gasoline prices, this implies a 10% increase in crude oil prices would raise headline CPI inflation by only 8bp. In contrast, oil-related sectors, i.e., oil and gas extraction and petrol processing, account for around 5% of the PPI basket, imply a 0.5pp increase in PPI from a 10% increase in crude oil prices. For natural gas, the CPI impact is difficult to quantify directly, as gas is not separately identified in the CPI basket and is instead embedded in broader utility categories. The gas supply sector accounts for 1.5% of the PPI basket, implying a smaller impact on PPI than oil-related sectors. Recall that Powell focused heavily on inflation developments and the outlook, more than potential concerns around the labor market. This skew gave a hawkish tone to the discussion. On inflation, Powell continued to focus on tariff-driven inflation in the core goods category. He noted that tariffs have likely added one -half to three -quarters of a percentage point to inflation and maintained the view that these effects are likely to begin to wane around the middle of the year. Powell argued that seeing core goods disinflation is “really important” for determining the potential for rate cuts in the back half of the year. Notably, Powell removed a line on disinflation for core services in his prepared remarks, potentially reflecting the strengthening in super core inflation that has occurred in recent months. When pressed on how the Fed is thinking about this category, Powell attributed the stickiness to a “bunch of idiosyncratic things”, and that they continue to expect progress to eventually return to this category. For our top charts for understanding the inflation outlook , see our latest chartbook: “US Inflation Outlook: Signs of stickiness even before oil shock”. Initially one would expect base metals prices to fall, and this appears to have occurred during the 1970s oil shocks. However, once the inflation starts to pass through the supply chain, the supply curve can shift up dramatically (with US average copper production costs rising by >50% between 1975 and 1981 nominally), and prices can rise despite lower demand levels (chart below). Copper is around 50% energy or linked costs, 50% labour, while nickel and aluminium costs are mainly energy or energy linked. However, supply remains vulnerable to further disruptions due to policy uncertainty (Zimbabwe export ban, China mining licences, etc.). Our previous expectation of a tight deficit market has reversed following significant downgrades to global EV assumptions. Front-loading of battery exports—particularly ESS in 1Q ahead of China’s cut to export rebates—has offset some of the EV weakness. Our demand forecasts include ~150ktpa of pipeline stocks, while our supply estimates incorporate a 5–8% disruption allowance. One of the Australian majors (see here, PLS, 2/19) has announced plans to restart a previously shuttered asset by 3Q’26, and we expect a few others to follow over the next 6–12 months. A key supply catalyst remains the restart of the Jianxiawo (JXW) mine, which we believe is likely to resume in summer 2026, adding an incremental 50–55kt LCE this year. With respect to Zimbabwe, we expect the suspension to be temporary, pending agreement on processes and commitments between the government and producers. records.text: 133 Thermal Coal – Supply direction is dependent on Indonesian quota policy Source: Citi Research, Wood Mackenzie, Bloomberg ■ Seaborne thermal coal demand outlook shows mixed signals in 2026 as the conflict in the Middle East supports coal demand via fuel switching. At the same time, prolonged conflict can weigh on global macro environment ultimately weighing on coal end use. Unfavourable gas plant economics can push utilities to switch to coal supporting demand. Prolonged conflict could ultimately add ~50- 70mt in our view to seaborne thermal coal demand based on fuel switching potential. At the same time, although not our base case, if the conflict in Middle East stretches further, global inflation expectations will get repriced weighing on macro sentiment. This in our view impacts industrial production ultimately reducing demand for coal. China and India have significantly improved their reliance on domestic coal since the Russia/Ukraine conflict. China has added ~800mt since 2022 while India has added ~200mt for the same period. We believe China and India will further focus on improving domestic output reducing pressure on seaborne coal markets. ■ Global seaborne thermal coal supply largely dependent on Indonesian quota policy. We see a ~10% y/y decline in Indonesian exports and an overall 7% y/y reduction in global seaborne supply. records.text: Agentic AI to meaningfully boost power demand from datacenters Most industry experts believe that the current pace of DC development is consistent with an adoption rate for Agentic AI of c.20-30% by 2030 (2035 for Europe). Yet, interviews with top executives from AI companies suggest that energy is seemingly the largest bottleneck in artificial intelligence. We believe these executives may be referring to the rising power needs from Agentic AI. We present several scenarios simulating a faster adoption of AI Agents; our analysis indicates that each +10 percentage point in adoption rates would increase the need for datacenters by +c.25%. By 2030-35, datacenters would account for c.20-25% of power demand in US and EU in our upside case. Growing share of AI Agents would meaningfully increase datacenter and energy needs United States. Based on expert calls we hosted, it is widely expected that by 2030, around 20-30% of queries will be Agentic. In other words, the current development of datacenters appears consistent with a slow and gradual take-up in Agentic AI. However, if we were to simulate a faster adoption rate for AI Agents, the current DC development would prove insufficient. On our analysis, each +10 pp in Agentic AI adoption rates could boost DC needs by +c.25% in the US by 2030. records.text: Long-Term Damage to Qatari LNG Supply Makes Room for US LNG in 2028/2029 To be clear, the long-term damage to 13 mtpa (3% of global LNG supply) of Qatari LNG supply, combined with our assumption that the upcoming Qatari LNG expansion train (North Field East T1) will be delayed a further three months (six months relative to our pre-conflict Oct26 expectation), does not reverse our bearish view of European gas and global LNG prices in the coming years. But it does delay and limit it. Specifically, we now only expect TTF to cross below 20 EUR/MWh in Summer 2028 (vs late 2027 prev.). Further, while we still expect NW European gas balances to face elevated congestion risks in 2028/2029 (and through 2032, for that matter), the scale of our estimated oversupply is significantly smaller, at 3%-9% of storage capacity, vs 30%-40% previously, significantly reducing the risk that global LNG supply needs to be curtailed in those years. As a result, we lift our 2028/2029 price forecasts to 19/16 EUR/MW for TTF (from 12/12 EUR), and to $6.90/$5.70/mmBtu for JKM (from $4.40/$4.45). Our revised LNG price forecasts leave our estimated US LNG export arb open, implying US LNG exports will continue to rise significantly during those years, driven by liquefaction plants currently under construction. (3) During the subsequent corrections, carry stayed persistently negative as IV decoupled from weakening RV, reflecting sustained demand for hedging and short- lived carry opportunities. (4) On late rebounds, SX5E surprisingly stopped bleeding, as RV squeezes higher, driven by positioning squeeze and re-risking flows positioning (see SX5E’s behaviour when EPI < 15). Key take away: In 2022, short-lived carry was tradable tactically; persistent hedging flows and repeated macro shocks kept vol sticky and made short-vol normalization less stable than in usual regimes. Banks Before the BoJ’s quantitative qualitative easing, banks were the largest holders of JGBs. As the BoJ scales back, banks are expected to act as the “next-door” buyer. In fact, after pension funds rebalanced by selling equities and foreign-currency assets and buying JGBs, banks have also been raising their holdings. However, the loan-deposit gap for banks is shrinking, and from an Asset-Liability-Management (ALM) perspective there is less incentive to hold long-dated bonds like 10–20 years JGBs. Consequently, the primary buyers of super-long JGBs are likely to be pension funds and foreign investors, while life insurers—the biggest super-long JGBs buyers in past—are now net sellers. The Cross-Border Equity Flow Indicator (xbEFI) measures the purchases and sales of equities by institutional investors, and is produced on a daily basis with a two day publication lag. The Cross -Border EFI focuses on trades by investors with base currencies that differ from a stock’s settlement currency. The indicator also includes transactions where the investor’s base currency is the same as the currency in which the trade is settled, and the settlement currency is different from that of the stock’s country of incorporation. An example of such a trade would be the purchase of a Dutch company’s American Depositary Receipts by a U.S. dollar-based fund. The Sovereign Bond Flow Indicator (SBFI) measures the purchases and sales of domestic and foreign sovereign bonds by institutional investors across countries and in regional aggregates and is available in unweighted and duration -weighted forms. We use unweighted flows in this document to capture the most relevant variable for a currency view. The SBFI is updated daily with a two-day publication lag. We use cross-border sovereign bond flows where available and total sovereign bond flows for all other countries.

Since last year, their purchases of super-long JGBs have been persistent, attracting not only hedge-fund flows but also real-money demand. A classic example is foreign central banks, which are said to hold safe assets when they manage foreign-exchange reserves. JPY-denominated assets make up 5.8% of all reported reserve holdings, according to the IMF’s Composite of Official Foreign Exchange Reserves database. Applying this percentage to total global reserves yields roughly USD438bn (about JPY68.6trn). records.text: 91 Aluminium – Middle East disruptions deepen an already tightening market Source: Citi Research, Wood Mackenzie, SMM, Bloomberg ■ We have been maintaining a structural bullish view on aluminium, reflecting constrained supply growth and tightening market balances, with prices already beginning to reflect this tightening backdrop earlier this year. The latest Middle East disruption should be seen in this context – not as a change to the structural thesis, but as an additional near-term catalyst that further tightens an already fragile system. In particular, risks around logistics disruption through the Strait of Hormuz and associated raw material constraints have the potential to amplify near-term price upside beyond our prior expectations. ■ We now embed a base case Middle East disruption into our balance, assuming c.~4Mt of capacity affected for ~2 months due to logistics-related raw material constraints, resulting in broader curtailments and pushing the market into a >1Mt deficit in 2026; outcomes remain highly duration dependent, with a prolonged disruption (e.g. extended Strait of Hormuz blockage) implying full shutdowns and longer restart timelines and a materially wider deficit extending into 2027, while we simultaneously revise demand growth lower to reflect higher energy prices, tighter financial conditions and softer end-use momentum. We close our long-standing 30y BTP–DSL tightener, opened in EGBs: Long 30y BTP vs short 30y DSL on 8 July, for a P&L of 1.6bp or EUR+32k (including accumulated positive carry). Prior to the conflict, the trade was previously deep in the money with over 30bp of accumulated P&L. In Europe: Energy shock prompts market paradigm shift , dated 20 March 2026, we argued that the developments in the Middle East have resulted in a paradigm shift, invalidating many of the assumptions we had embedded in our previous forecasts for spreads, resulting in an outlook with lower real GDP growth, ECB rate hikes, higher volatility and a regime shift away from carry trades. We see risks skewed towards a further escalation, which could see BTP spreads widen even further from here. Considering all this, we close the trade now. records.text: Our commodities team further raised their energy price forecasts in light of the n ongoing conflict in the Middle East. The team now expects shipping through the Strait of Hormuz to remain at only 5% of normal levels for 6 weeks (vs 3 weeks before). As a result, they now see high energy prices for longer with Brent and TTF gas prices at $80 and 40 EUR/MWh in 2026Q4 (vs $71 and 34 EUR/MWh before). Risks remain tilted to the upside and we again set out adverse and severely adverse energy price scenarios. We downgrade Euro area growth by a further 0.3pp over the next year, taking n the peak GDP level hit to 0.7% relative to the pre-war forecast (from 0.4% before) and lower Q4/Q4 growth to 0.7% (from 1% before and 1.4% before the war). We now see headline inflation peaking at 3.2% in Q2 (vs 2.9% previously and 2.0% before the war) and expect core inflation to rise to 2.5% in Q3 (vs 2.4% previously and 2.2% before the war), with slightly more persistence in core inflation given the bigger magnitude of the energy shock. Risks to our new forecast are skewed towards lower growth and higher inflation. Given persistent upward pressure on energy prices, higher core inflation and n hawkish post-meeting communication, we now expect the ECB to hike policy rates by 25bp at the April and June meetings (with the deposit rate reaching a peak 2.5% in June). Turbulence is a price-based measure of the joint unusualness of G10 currency returns. records.text: See Appendix A-1 for Analyst Certification, Important Disclosures and Research Analyst Affiliations. 23 Mar 2026 05:57:35 ET │ 9 pages Japan Economics First tally of Shunto spring wage negotiations: A strong start CITI'S TAKE The first tally of spring wage negotiation results shows an average wage hike agreed upon thus far of 5.26%. This is slightly lower than the historic 5.46% increase agreed upon as of the first-round last year but marks a third consecutive year of 5%+ hikes. We think the result is strong and should help the trend for wage hikes to be firmly established. The base pay increase was 3.85% (+3.84% in the first-round last year). We feel the development of spring wage negotiations this year has been positive for the BoJ, as it was last year, but the result will probably in line with its expectations and thus looks unlikely to speed up the pace of policy normalization. Moreover, given that the escalating Middle East situation was hardly factored into the latest result, we do not see the wage hike results as convincing grounds to expect an early rate hike. In the UK, expectations have risen but have since stabilized; in the Eurozone, they are falling from recent highs; and in the US, inflation swaps are net lower on the month. Taken together, the signal is not one of a persistent, war‑driven inflation problem. Meanwhile, growth expectations have begun to roll over. This is particularly important for economies such as the UK and Eurozone, where limited growth was already priced in to begin with, suggesting that the recent hawkish repricing may have gone too far. To make it clear, we do not mean to imply hikes will not occur, we only want to make the point that in some cases, the central bank reaction function may ultimately prove to be either slower or less forceful than markets are currently indicating given counterbalanced risks to growth. Both the GBP and EUR stand out in that regard. In the UK, BoE pricing shifted more than any other developed central bank, but markets have already begun to unwind some of that hawkishness as it becomes clear that expectations may have overshot (Figure 4). By contrast, ECB pricing remains near last week’s peak and appears to be overlooking deteriorating growth expectations. records.text: Oil prices have risen sharply since late February after the start of the Middle East n conflict. Against this backdrop, clients have increasingly asked about the implications for China’s inflation outlook, especially following 41 consecutive months of year-over-year PPI deflation. Since January, we have raised our 2026 full-year CPI and PPI forecasts from 0.6% and -0.7% to 0.9% and 0.8%, respectively, and now raise both to 1.0% on the back of our commodity team’s latest oil price forecast update, with year-over-year PPI inflation likely turning positive in March or April. Upside risks remain, given the potential for further non-linear moves in energy markets. We first examine China’s exposure to energy shocks and the transmission of oil n and natural gas prices into domestic inflation. While China is a large net importer of oil and natural gas, its effective exposure to Hormuz disruptions appears more limited than headline import dependence suggests. Around 30% of crude oil supply is linked to flows through the Strait of Hormuz (vs. around 70% total oil import dependence), and only around 6% of natural gas supply is exposed via LNG imports (vs. around 40% natural gas import dependence). Moreover, China’s energy consumption mix, with relatively low reliance on oil and gas compared with other major economies, further dampens pass-through to domestic inflation.
