records.text: ated market structure for rare earth materials. Dual-use technology: built for defence, adopted for civilian use The next decade will see increased adoption of drones for civilian uses. In agriculture, drones cut spraying costs by ~70%, reduce spraying time by more than 90%, and lower water use by roughly 90%. In logistics and delivery, they halve inventory processing time and enable last-mile deliveries in under 20 minutes. Drones civilian applications are set to gain market share Defence has repeatedly acted as an early incubator for advanced technologies, funding systems that prioritise robustness, autonomy and performance. These technologies often diffuse into civilian markets once costs fall and reliability improves. GPS, developed by the US Department of Defense for military navigation, later became ubiquitous in cars and smartphones; computer vision, originally designed for target recognition and missile guidance, now underpins facial recognition and biometrics. The same pattern is visible in robotics: iRobot, widely regarded as the pioneer of consumer robotics, began by developing robots for space exploration and military use, while Boston Dynamics, now a global leader in humanoid robotics, traces its flagship platforms to disaster-response and defence-related research. Drones are following a similar trajectory. While defence has historically been the main application and a key growth driver, civilian uses are set to take a larger share over the next decade. However, large companies take up a disproportionate share of union members affiliated with JTUC, meaning that the average wage increase will be unlikely to change significantly even as settlements at SMEs are increasingly added to the aggregate number. As a rule of thumb, in an average year wage hikes are revised downward by only 0.2ppt from the first tally to the final tally in July. Based on this we think wage and base pay hikes will be around 5.0% in the final tally this year. We think that the key point to watch in terms of the implications of spring wage negotiations will be on how settlements with the seven million union members of JTUC spill over to the macro wages of Japan’s 62 million workers including non- union members. In particular, wage growth for workers at many SMEs and non- regular workers, which are not included in the JTUC figures, is likely to be indispensable to boosting the overall economy. If wage hikes for SMEs remain strong in upcoming settlements, scheduled cash earnings (basic macro wages) may well be stronger than the JTUC tally suggests. In this paper we test the usefulness of MRP for estimating alpha-decay that we observe between the IS and out-of-sample (OOS) Sharpe measurements in most systematic strategies. Our first paper of this series, Estimating the ‘true’ Sharpe ratio of systematic strategies, dated 20 September 2024, introduced a Bayesian framework for estimating the Sharpe ratio. This framework allows us to consistently update our prior view of the Sharpe ratio (the IS view) as soon as new OOS data becomes available. We showed how a probabilistic view of performance can be turned into a live ‘health-dashboard’. By treating the Sharpe ratio as a random variable with a sensible prior and updating that prior with in-sample and then live observations, the resulting posterior distribution captures both the point-estimate of the ‘true’ Sharpe and the uncertainty that surrounds it. Our second piece of this series, Predicting alpha decay in systematic strategies, dated 4 September 2025, focused on the systematic erosion of performance once a strategy is published. We identified three robust drivers of alpha decay: i) high sensitivity to outliers in the backtest, ii) the sign and magnitude of a ‘robust-skewness’ metric and, iii) an elevated IS Sharpe, which paradoxically forewarns of a larger post-launch slip. South Pars/North Dome is the world's largest natural gas field, containing an estimated 51 trillion cubic meters of gas and 40 billion barrels of condensate, shared between Iran and Qatar. By targeting this facility, the conflict has moved beyond conventional military operations to direct- ly threatening the backbone of global energy supply. Building on this earlier work, we now turn our attention to the MRP metric as a potential means to better quantify strategy decay risk. Financial strategies do not evolve in a static environment: correlations shift, market microstructure changes, and behavioural inefficiencies tend to be arbitraged away. As a result, performance in one period may not generalise to another. From an allocator’s perspective, the central question is therefore not simply the average Sharpe ratio, but how far risk-adjusted performance could decline when market conditions change. The Minimum Regime Performance (MRP) framework Introduced by Nolan Alexander and Frank J. Fabozzi in a paper published earlier this year (Journal of Portfolio Management, 2026, Vol 52, Issue 4) addresses this issue by partitioning a strategy’s return history into several internally consistent sub-periods representing different market environments. In practice, the methodology searches across all admissible ways of splitting the return series into segments of sufficient length. Our estimates suggest that a 10% increase in oil prices raises PPI inflation by 0.5pp on average in 12 months, while lifting CPI inflation by only about 0.1pp. The response of PPI is front-loaded, with a modest initial impact followed by an overshoot after 2 months, before gradually moderating after six months. These estimates are based on supply-driven oil shocks, which tend to have less persistent effects than demand-driven shocks. We also cross-check our results based on oil’s weight in the CPI and PPI baskets, yielding broadly similar results. The limited pass-through to consumer prices also reflects China’s domestic fuel pricing mechanism, which dampens the transmission. Energy-led cost-push inflation may not translate into a broad-based reflation n dynamic. Historical experience suggests that energy-driven PPI reflation is highly concentrated in upstream industrial sectors, accounting for roughly 80% of headline PPI gains (despite only around 30% weight in the PPI basket). records.text: 23 March 2026 Focus Germany Page 2 Deutsche Bank AG A look at the MoF's March 2026 Monthly Report In this update, we take a look at the March 2026 Monthly Report from the Federal Ministry of Finance (MoF), which contains the financial statistics data on federal budget developments for the first two month of the year. The analysis builds on our previous work regarding Germany's fiscal policy shift (see also here and here). It considers the latest dynamics of a) the federal government's core budget as well as b) the two major off-budgetary funds SV BW (Federal Armed Forces Fund) and SV IK (Infrastructure & Climate Protection Fund) for which the government provides monthly credit stock/flow data.1 The MoF's February 2026 budget print Monthly budgetary developments in a nutshell As Figure 1 illustrates, on a 12-month smoothed basis, the total federal financing deficit – comprising the core budget, the SV BW and the SV IK – continued to increase moderately further in February, to nearly EUR 130 bn (from about EUR 124 bn in January; + EUR 5.6 bn). Hence, based on the trailing twelve-month sum, the total deficit has thus widened by close to EUR 70 bn since the effective entry into force of the 2025 federal budget last October. Turning to monthly data, the total deficit amounted to about EUR 9 bn in February (January: c. EUR 34 bn). Even though this represents a marked decrease over the month, this deficit reduction was within the range of usual seasonal fluctuations (see Figure 2).

The reasoning is simple. While the textbook response would be to “look through” the inflationary impact as “transitory”, this relies on one very important assumption: that long-term inflation expectations are well anchored. Anchored inflation expectations can no longer be taken for granted, with the current energy-driven inflation shock being the fourth successive price shock in the past five years (the post -pandemic reopening, Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and 2025’s Liberation Day tariffs being the others). With that, there are risks of inflation expectations destabilizing, with second-round effects from higher energy prices potentially driving an upward consumer-price spiral. Although the negative energy impulse to GDP growth is more contained in the US than elsewhere, it comes alongside two other reasons to expect a cyclical slowdown in the remainder of the year. First, the fiscal boost to growth from the provisions of last summer’s fiscal law—including the middle-class tax cuts and full expensing of manufacturing investment—is likely to fade in H2. Our BRS was created in 2003, giving us a meaningful set of historical analogues to assess how market shocks feed through to allocation decisions. While there is no perfect comparison, Russia’s invasion of Ukraine is the closest parallel at this stage, as such it’s telling that 1m after Russia’s invasion, investors had increased their risk exposure relative to the start of the war. Historically, risk positioning unwinds most sharply and most quickly during episodes that simultaneously impair liquidity and gr owth (notably Lehman/GFC and Covid). As such, today’s positioning score of + 6 implies asymmetric downside risk if positions were to unwind, given there is still room to sell. However, unless the Iran conflict materially freezes funding markets and undermines growth, positioning is unlikely to move meaningfully below neutral. That s aid, we remain well above neutral today, suggesting that until positioning normalizes, overweight risk exposure continues to represent a key vulnerability. Indonesia ore quota restraint through 1H’26 may ease through 2H’26, but higher energy should provide cost support for NPI, limiting price downside and resulting in a more balanced global nickel market outlook at current $17k/t price levels. We think both nickel supply (via Indonesia policy) and nickel demand (through battery material substitution) look reasonably price elastic and it is difficult to see prices sustainably breaking out of a $16-20k/t range. ■ In our bear scenario (20% probability) prices average $14 k/t for the rest of 2026. This assumes minimal disruptions or constraints on further Indonesian supply growth and/or an incrementally bearish global growth backdrop (with softer China stainless steel demand and broader risk-off behaviour). Automakers accelerate and deepen a pivot to non-nickel LFP chemistries. ■ In our bull scenario (30% probability) prices average $20k/t through year-end. We expect China silver imports to be healthy in 2026. The silver inventory on SHFE declined by 11moz YTD in 2026 driven by strong demand for physical silver. The solar PV and investment demand are driving demand in China. We expect solar PV demand to gradually decline in 2026. First due to continued silver thrifting/substitution in solar cell. records.text: E M – L O C A L E YE S FO R A G L O B A L V IE W 224/03/2026 Going into more detail, the MRP methodology evaluates how a strategy’s risk-adjusted performance behaves across different market conditions by dividing its historical return series into several non-overlapping sub-periods. Within each sub-period, a standard risk-adjusted metric – the Sharpe ratio – is calculated. For every admissible way of partitioning the data (subject to a minimum length constraint), the lowest Sharpe ratio observed across the resulting segments is recorded, and the overall MRP corresponds to the minimum of these values across all possible partitions. In essence, MRP provides a conservative estimate of the weakest level of risk- adjusted performance a strategy may experience under plausible structural market environments. In applying this framework to our own QIS universe, we imposed a one-year minimum length for every sub- period. For each strategy we first identified the total number of observations available in the backtest window and then generated every feasible combination of splits that respects the one-year minimum. For each admissible number of splits, we computed the corresponding MRP and retained the configuration that produced the lowest MRP; when multiple configurations yielded the same minimum value, we selected the one with the fewest regime boundaries (see Quant Corner opposite). Foreign hedging across G10 currencies has increased, most notably in the NZD, where hedge ratios have risen to 74%, levels last seen in May. The clear exception is the USD: the foreign hedge ratio has fallen nearly 3 percentage points to 56%. In effect, the foreign hedge ratio signal is long USD and short the rest of G10. Domestic hedging signals are more mixed. European, Canadian, and U.S. investors have increased hedging of foreign FX exposure, while Australian and UK investors have reduced hedging activity. Australian flows are particularly notable: the domestic hedge ratio stands at 83%, near highs last seen in 2023, suggesting that any further reduction would provide a positive tailwind for the AUD. Taken together, both foreign and domestic hedging activity support a short GBP position, while the opposite is true for the USD. For now, the long USD trend remains well supported by real money flows.
